1	<p align="center">

4	
5	# deadreckon
6	
7	**The control plane for unattended agentic coding CLIs.**
8	
9	deadreckon runs long coding tasks the way you wish agentic CLIs already did: in an isolated workspace, with durable state, live attach, spend and wall-clock caps, per-turn undo, provenance, traces, self-documenting run artifacts, and a signed acceptance gate before anything is promoted.
10	
11	It is not trying to out-code Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, GitHub Copilot CLI, or the next terminal agent. Use the agentic CLI you already trust. deadreckon wraps it in the missing operational harness.
12	
13	```bash
14	deadreckon run "replace the legacy billing flow with Stripe Checkout"
15	deadreckon attach latest
16	deadreckon status
17	deadreckon doc latest
18	deadreckon finish latest
19	deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
20	```
21	
22	## Why "deadreckon"?
23	
24	Dead reckoning is navigation without perfect visibility: start from a known
25	position, keep a continuous record of movement, and use that record to know
26	where you are now.
27	
28	That is the problem with unattended coding agents. The model is probabilistic,
29	the task can run for a long time, context is partial, and the terminal may be
30	gone by the time you inspect the result. deadreckon keeps the course anyway:
31	every turn writes state, spend, traces, provenance, snapshots, docs, and
32	acceptance evidence.
33	
34	The name is the contract: do not trust a final answer alone. Navigate agent work
35	by evidence.
36	
37	## Why This Exists
38	
39	Agentic coding CLIs are good at the inner loop: talk to a model, inspect files, run commands, edit code, and produce a patch. Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, GitHub Copilot CLI, and similar tools are racing on model UX, tool UX, context handling, and terminal/editor ergonomics.
40	
41	deadreckon focuses on the layer around that CLI: the unattended run lifecycle.
42	
43	The painful part of unattended coding is different:
44	
45	- Where exactly did the agent run?
46	- What did it spend?
47	- Which files did each turn touch?
48	- Can I attach after closing my laptop?
49	- Can I kill it without leaving orphaned processes?
50	- Can I resume after a crash?
51	- Can I undo turn 7 without rolling back the whole project?
52	- Can I prove the agent did not mark its own work as accepted?
53	- Can I apply the result only after I inspect it?
54	
55	deadreckon is built around those questions. It treats an agentic CLI as the worker, then adds the control plane that makes unattended work reviewable, recoverable, auditable, and safe to apply.
56	
57	## The Printing Press Contract
58	
59	deadreckon borrows a simple idea from the CLI Printing Press pattern: split
60	judgment from enforcement.
61	
62	The agentic CLI and Markdown skills own the judgment layer: what to inspect,
63	what to try, what to edit, and when to say the work is done. The Rust binary owns
64	the enforcement layer: state, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, cancellation,
65	snapshots, provenance, spend, traces, gates, promotion, and recovery.
66	
67	That split matters. The agent can write code, but it cannot forge completion,
68	skip the audit trail, bypass run state, or silently publish its own work.
69	
70	## The Unique Feature Set
71	
72	### Isolated Worktrees By Default
73	
74	In a git repo, `deadreckon run` creates a separate `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch under `~/.deadreckon/worktrees/`. Your checkout is left untouched until you explicitly run:
75	
76	```bash
77	deadreckon apply <run-id>
78	```
79	
80	Run ids accept unique prefixes, and most commands also accept `latest` for the
81	newest run in the current project.
82	
83	You can also run in copy mode, fresh mode, or explicit in-place mode:
84	
85	```bash
86	deadreckon run "goal" --from .
87	deadreckon run "goal" --fresh
88	deadreckon run "goal" --in-place --i-know-its-a-lot
89	```
90	
91	### Wrap The Agentic CLI You Already Use
92	
93	deadreckon routes turns through configurable providers. Today, the first-class local CLI adapters are:
94	
95	- `cli:codex`
96	- `cli:claude-code`
97	
98	It also supports direct model routes:
99	
100	- `anthropic`
101	- `openai`
102	- OpenAI-compatible endpoints
103	- `--smoke` for keyless local verification
104	
105	That means subscription users can route through supported local agentic CLIs, while API users can route through direct HTTP providers. The CLI does the coding; deadreckon owns the run boundary around it.
106	
107	### Durable State After Every Turn
108	
109	Each run writes a complete local record under `~/.deadreckon/runstate/`:
110	
111	```text
112	state.json
113	history.json
114	events.jsonl
115	traces.jsonl
116	spend.jsonl
117	provenance.jsonl
118	snapshots/turn-<N>/
119	proofs/turn-acceptance.json
120	working/ or promoted library artifact
121	```
122	
123	If the terminal dies, the run state is still there. If a provider call completes, the trace is there. If a tool edits a file, the provenance is there.
124	
125	### Live Attach Without Owning The Process
126	
127	Start a run, walk away, then attach from another terminal:
128	
129	```bash
130	deadreckon attach latest
131	```
132	
133	The TUI shows compact run status, phase, goal, working directory, per-turn timer,
134	spend or context telemetry, provider/tool activity, generated files, process
135	status, and completion actions. Completed runs can toggle a styled Markdown
136	rendering of `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` directly in the main panel.
137	
138	Detach without killing the run:
139	
140	```text
141	Ctrl-D
142	```
143	
144	### Spend And Wall-Clock Guardrails
145	
146	Every provider response appends a spend record and updates totals. API routes track token cost. Subscription CLI routes can be capped by wall-clock time.
147	
148	```bash
149	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-spend 15
150	deadreckon run "large refactor" --max-wall-seconds 1800
151	```
152	
153	High spend requires explicit confirmation, so scripts do not accidentally launch expensive runs.
154	
155	### Per-Turn Undo
156	
157	deadreckon snapshots the working directory at turn boundaries:
158	
159	```bash
160	deadreckon undo --run <run-id>
161	deadreckon undo --run <run-id> --turn 3
162	```
163	
164	This is not just `git reset`. It works against the run's own snapshot trail and records the undo in the run trace.
165	
166	### Signed Acceptance Gates
167	
168	The agent cannot declare its own work accepted.
169	
170	Completion requires a marker written by the separate `dr-gate` binary and bound to the run id with a run-local nonce. deadreckon refuses forged or self-written markers.
171	
172	Default acceptance checks that the working directory exists and runs `cargo test` when `Cargo.toml` is present. You can add an explicit `acceptance.yaml`:
173	
174	```yaml
175	name: notes check
176	checks:
177	  - kind: file_exists
178	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
179	  - kind: content_match
180	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
181	    pattern: "dead reckoning"
182	  - kind: build_success
183	    cwd: "{working_dir}"
184	```
185	
186	Supported check kinds:
187	
188	```text
189	cargo_test
190	file_exists
191	content_match
192	build_success
193	```
194	
195	### Provenance, Traces, And Run Docs
196	
197	deadreckon records which model/tool call touched which files, then writes self-documenting artifacts for the completed run:
198	
199	```bash
200	deadreckon doc <run-id>
201	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind as-built
202	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind decisions
203	deadreckon doc <run-id> --kind delta
204	```
205	
206	Each accepted run produces a review packet:
207	
208	- `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` explains what happened.
209	- `RUN-AS-BUILT.md` captures the subsystem shape after the run.
210	- `RUN-DECISIONS.md` records meaningful decisions.
211	- `AS-BUILT-DELTA.md` proposes architecture-doc updates when the run is broad enough.
212	- `manifest.json` records the promoted artifact identity and provenance hash.
213	
214	Agentic CLIs usually leave you with a patch and a transcript. deadreckon turns
215	the session into a local published artifact you can inspect, materialize, extend,
216	or apply.
217	
218	### Resume, Kill, Extend, Materialize
219	
220	Runs are lifecycle objects, not one terminal session:
221	
222	```bash
223	deadreckon list
224	deadreckon status
225	deadreckon show latest
226	deadreckon kill latest
227	deadreckon resume latest
228	deadreckon resume latest --from-turn 2
229	deadreckon extend latest "add tests and polish the UI"
230	deadreckon finish latest
231	deadreckon export latest --dest ./finished-project
232	deadreckon cleanup --completed
233	```
234	
235	Resume reconstructs history from durable traces and ignores incomplete trailing trace entries.
236	
237	## The Mental Model
238	
239	```text
240	your repo
241	  |
242	  | deadreckon run "goal"
243	  v
244	isolated worktree or copy
245	  |
246	  | provider route: cli:codex, cli:claude-code, anthropic, openai, compatible
247	  v
248	sandboxed turn loop
249	  |
250	  | every turn: trace, spend, provenance, snapshot, docs
251	  v
252	signed acceptance gate
253	  |
254	  | inspect, doc, apply, discard, extend, export, cleanup
255	  v
256	your branch or artifact
257	```
258	
259	deadreckon owns the boring but load-bearing parts: state, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, cancellation, snapshots, provenance, gates, and promotion.
260	
261	The agent owns the coding work.
262	
263	## The Trust Contract
264	
265	With deadreckon, `completed` means more than "the agent stopped." It means:
266	
267	- the run state was persisted
268	- the work happened in an isolated workspace
269	- spend and traces were written
270	- file provenance was recorded
271	- snapshots exist for rollback
272	- run docs were generated
273	- `dr-gate` signed acceptance
274	- the artifact was promoted atomically
275	
276	That is the difference between an agent transcript and an auditable run.
277	
278	## Quickstart
279	
280	Build the release binary:
281	
282	```bash
283	cargo build --release
284	```
285	
286	Initialize local config:
287	
288	```bash
289	./target/release/deadreckon init
290	```
291	
292	Run a task:
293	
294	```bash
295	./target/release/deadreckon run "make a realtime chess app"
296	```
297	
298	Attach to the run:
299	
300	```bash
301	./target/release/deadreckon attach <run-id>
302	```
303	
304	Inspect the result:
305	
306	```bash
307	./target/release/deadreckon show <run-id>
308	./target/release/deadreckon doc <run-id>
309	```
310	
311	Apply a completed worktree run:
312	
313	```bash
314	./target/release/deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
315	```
316	
317	## Keyless Smoke Test
318	
319	Use `--smoke` to prove the harness works without API keys or subscription-backed CLIs:
320	
321	```bash
322	DEADRECKON_HOME=$PWD/.deadreckon-smoke \
323	  ./target/release/deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" \
324	  --smoke \
325	  --sandbox none \
326	  --max-spend 1
327	```
328	
329	This still exercises the real turn loop, sandbox dispatch, snapshots, spend records, traces, provenance, docs, and acceptance gate. The only fake part is the provider response.
330	
331	## Normal Coding Run
332	
333	After `init`, the default path in a git repo is:
334	
335	```bash
336	deadreckon run "make a full task productivity tracker in nodejs that allows me to manage my day"
337	deadreckon attach latest
338	deadreckon status
339	deadreckon doc latest
340	deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
341	```
342	
343	`run` prints the run id and attach command immediately:
344	
345	```text
346	started run <short-id> (<full-id>)
347	attach: deadreckon attach <short-id>
348	```
349	
350	Before creating state or files, `run` prints a preview showing the mode, branch, base ref, and worktree path. Use `--preview` to print the preview and exit.
351	
352	## Provider Configuration
353	
354	Examples:
355	
356	```bash
357	deadreckon init --provider cli:codex --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
358	deadreckon init --provider cli:claude-code --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
359	deadreckon init --provider anthropic --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
360	deadreckon init --provider openai --api-key "$OPENAI_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
361	```
362	
363	Inspect or edit config:
364	
365	```bash
366	deadreckon config get defaults.provider
367	deadreckon config provider
368	deadreckon config provider cli:codex
369	deadreckon config model
370	deadreckon config model gpt-5.1-codex --provider cli:codex
371	deadreckon config set defaults.max_spend 15
372	deadreckon config set defaults.sandbox auto
373	deadreckon config set providers.anthropic.api_key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
374	```
375	
376	Before a run, `deadreckon run --preview "goal"` shows the provider route and
377	model that will be used. For one run, override both directly:
378	
379	```bash
380	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:codex --model gpt-5.1-codex
381	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:claude-code --model sonnet
382	```
383	
384	Runtime config defaults to:
385	
386	```text
387	~/.deadreckon/config.toml
388	```
389	
390	Set `DEADRECKON_HOME` for isolated local runs or tests.
391	
392	## Sandbox Backends
393	
394	Supported backends:
395	
396	```text
397	auto
398	sandbox-exec
399	bwrap
400	docker
401	none
402	```
403	
404	`auto` chooses `sandbox-exec` on macOS when available and `bwrap` on Linux when available. `docker` is opt-in. `none` is explicit and warns because it is unsafe for real unattended work.
405	
406	Check the current machine:
407	
408	```bash
409	deadreckon doctor
410	```
411	
412	## Compared With Agentic Coding CLIs
413	
414	deadreckon is not a replacement for agentic CLIs like Amp, Rovo Dev, Cursor CLI, Codex, Claude Code, Aider, deepseek-tui, or GitHub Copilot CLI. It is the supervisor you put around that class of tool when the task is too long, risky, or expensive for "run the agent in my checkout and hope I can reconstruct what happened."
415	
416	| Operational concern | Agentic CLI alone | deadreckon supervising the CLI |
417	|---|---|---|
418	| Workspace safety | Often runs where you start it | Creates an isolated worktree by default and leaves your checkout untouched |
419	| Long-running attach | Usually tied to the current terminal session | Run state is durable; attach from another terminal later |
420	| Process control | Kill/resume behavior varies by tool | Tracks child PIDs, kills live work, resumes from durable state |
421	| Spend control | Token/cost visibility varies by provider | Writes `spend.jsonl`, tracks totals, enforces spend and wall-clock caps |
422	| Undo | Usually git-level or manual | Snapshots every turn and restores a specific turn with `deadreckon undo` |
423	| Provenance | Conversation history may not map cleanly to file changes | Records model/tool/file linkage in `provenance.jsonl` |
424	| Observability | Tool logs are tool-specific | Writes normalized `events.jsonl`, `traces.jsonl`, spend, docs, and run state |
425	| Acceptance | The agent may declare itself done | Requires a signed `dr-gate` marker before promotion |
426	| Applying work | Patch review/apply flow is tool-specific | `apply`, `discard`, `export`, `extend`, and `cleanup` are first-class lifecycle actions |
427	| Multi-run coordination | Usually left to the operator | Scope/task locks prevent conflicting same-task runs |
428	
429	Use the agentic CLI for intelligence. Use deadreckon for isolation, supervision, evidence, recovery, and promotion.
430	
431	## Command Surface
432	
433	```text
434	init          create local config
435	config        inspect or edit config keys
436	run           start an unattended coding run
437	attach        open the live dashboard
438	status/next   show the current project's latest run and next action
439	list          show current-project runs by default; --all shows every scope
440	show          inspect state, lineage, spend, files
441	doc           print or export run documentation
442	finish/done   choose apply or export from the completed run mode
443	apply         apply a completed worktree run to your branch
444	keep          alias for apply
445	abandon       remove a worktree run and temporary branch
446	discard       alias for abandon
447	materialize   copy a completed artifact to a normal directory
448	export        alias for materialize
449	cleanup       clean abandoned, stale, or completed worktrees
450	prune         alias for cleanup
451	extend        continue from a completed run
452	follow-up     alias for extend
453	resume        continue an interrupted run
454	continue      alias for resume
455	kill          stop a live run and child processes
456	stop          alias for kill
457	undo          restore a previous turn snapshot
458	import        normalize histories from other coding tools
459	doctor        check config, providers, sandboxes, disk, runtime
460	```
461	
462	## Verification
463	
464	Full local verification:
465	
466	```bash
467	make verify
468	```
469	
470	Useful targeted checks:
471	
472	```bash
473	make build
474	make smoke
475	make doctor
476	STRESS_SECONDS=30 make stress
477	```
478	
479	The workspace test suite covers provider routing, mock OpenAI-compatible runs, CLI-provider wrappers, kill/resume behavior, signed gates, snapshots, provenance/trace linkage, worktree/copy/in-place modes, lifecycle actions, docs generation, and multi-run locking.
480	
481	## Status
482	
483	deadreckon is alpha software. The core lifecycle is implemented and tested, but the project is intentionally conservative about claims: local-first state, worktree isolation, provider routing, sandbox dispatch, durable traces/spend/provenance, signed gates, undo, docs, apply/abandon/materialize/extend, and smoke verification are the current product.
484	
485	The V1 candidate list is deliberately short. The biggest known next feature is explicit sub-agent forking:
486	
487	```text
488	deadreckon fork <run-id> --prompt "..."
489	```
490

1	# deadreckon HOWTO
2	
3	This repo builds a Rust CLI named `deadreckon` for unattended coding runs.
4	The CLI is the control plane; the TUI is an attachable live dashboard.
5	
6	## Build And Install Alias
7	
8	```bash
9	cd /Users/gdc/deadreckon
10	make build
11	make alias-zsh
12	source /Users/gdc/.zshrc
13	deadreckon --help
14	```
15	
16	The alias points to:
17	
18	```bash
19	/Users/gdc/deadreckon/target/release/deadreckon
20	```
21	
22	## Make Targets
23	
24	```bash
25	make help             # list targets
26	make build            # cargo build --release
27	make verify           # release build, tests, clippy, fmt check
28	make smoke            # keyless local smoke run
29	make doctor           # run deadreckon doctor
30	make stress           # 5 concurrent runs; defaults to 10 minutes
31	make clean-runtime    # remove repo-local smoke state
32	```
33	
34	Override runtime locations or stress duration:
35	
36	```bash
37	DEADRECKON_HOME=/tmp/deadreckon-home make smoke
38	STRESS_SECONDS=30 make stress
39	```
40	
41	## Runtime State
42	
43	By default, deadreckon writes runtime state to:
44	
45	```bash
46	/Users/gdc/.deadreckon
47	```
48	
49	For disposable tests, set:
50	
51	```bash
52	export DEADRECKON_HOME=/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.try-deadreckon
53	```
54	
55	Per-run artifacts include:
56	
57	```text
58	state.json
59	history.json
60	events.jsonl
61	traces.jsonl
62	spend.jsonl
63	provenance.jsonl
64	snapshots/turn-<N>/
65	proofs/turn-acceptance.json
66	working/ or library/<scope>/<run-id>/
67	```
68	
69	Completed accepted runs are promoted to:
70	
71	```bash
72	/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/library/<scope>/<run-id>/
73	```
74	
75	The directory where you launch `deadreckon run` is recorded as `launch-dir`.
76	In a git repo, the normal default is a separate worktree on a `dr/...` branch.
77	Your checkout is left unchanged until `deadreckon apply <run-id>`.
78	
79	## First Run
80	
81	Interactive setup:
82	
83	```bash
84	deadreckon init
85	deadreckon doctor
86	```
87	
88	Non-interactive examples:
89	
90	```bash
91	deadreckon init --provider cli:codex --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
92	deadreckon init --provider anthropic --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
93	deadreckon init --provider openai --api-key "$OPENAI_API_KEY" --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
94	```
95	
96	Inspect or edit config:
97	
98	```bash
99	deadreckon config get defaults.provider
100	deadreckon config provider

102	deadreckon config model
103	deadreckon config model gpt-5.1-codex --provider cli:codex
104	deadreckon config set defaults.max_spend 15
105	deadreckon config set defaults.sandbox auto
106	deadreckon config set providers.anthropic.api_key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
107	```

109	## Keyless Smoke Run
110	
111	Use this to prove the harness works without provider keys:
112	
113	```bash
114	export DEADRECKON_HOME=/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.try-deadreckon
115	rm -rf "$DEADRECKON_HOME"
116	
117	deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" --smoke --sandbox none --max-spend 1
118	deadreckon list
119	deadreckon status
120	```
121	
122	The default list is compact, project-scoped, and shows eight-character run IDs.
123	Commands accept unique prefixes, so `deadreckon show 861c51bf` works when that
124	prefix is unique. Most run-id arguments also accept `latest` or `last`, resolved
125	to the latest run for the current project. Use `--all` for global history and
126	`--full` for scripts or exact-copy output.
127	
128	Capture the latest full run id:
129	
130	```bash
131	RUN_ID=$(deadreckon list --full | awk 'NR==2 {print $1}')
132	```
133	
134	Then inspect it:
135	
136	```bash
137	deadreckon show "$RUN_ID"
138	deadreckon attach latest
139	```

141	## Normal Coding Run
142	
143	After `init`, the normal path in a git repo is:
144	
145	```bash
146	deadreckon run "make a full task productivity tracker in nodejs that allows me to manage my day"
147	deadreckon attach latest
148	deadreckon status
149	deadreckon finish latest
150	deadreckon apply latest --autostash --cleanup
151	```
152	
153	`run` prints the run id and attach command as soon as state is created:
154	
155	```text
156	started run <short-id> (<full-id>)
157	attach: deadreckon attach <short-id>
158	```
159	
160	Before it creates state or files, `run` prints a preview. In a clean git repo,
161	the preview shows `mode: worktree`, the `dr/...` branch, the base ref, and the
162	worktree path. Use `--yes` to skip the confirmation in scripts or `--preview`
163	to print the block and exit.
164	
165	Mode overrides:
166	
167	```bash
168	deadreckon run "goal" --fresh                         # old empty working dir
169	deadreckon run "goal" --from .                        # gitignore-aware copy
170	deadreckon run "goal" --worktree                      # force git worktree
171	deadreckon run "goal" --base main --branch dr/my-task # customize worktree branch
172	deadreckon run "goal" --allow-dirty                   # seed dirty files into worktree
173	deadreckon run "goal" --in-place --i-know-its-a-lot   # edit current dir directly
174	```
175	
176	Outside git, interactive `run` offers git init, copy mode, or cancel.
177	Non-interactive runs outside git need an explicit mode:
178	
179	```bash
180	deadreckon run "goal" --from . --yes
181	deadreckon run "goal" --fresh --yes
182	git init && deadreckon run "goal" --yes
183	```
184	
185	The default config from `deadreckon init` supplies the provider, sandbox, `$10` spend cap, and `3600` second wall-clock cap. Use flags only when overriding those defaults:
186	
187	```bash
188	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:codex
189	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:codex --model gpt-5.1-codex
190	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:claude-code
191	deadreckon run "goal" --provider cli:claude-code --model sonnet
192	deadreckon run "goal" --provider anthropic
193	deadreckon run "goal" --provider openai
194	deadreckon run "goal" --sandbox sandbox-exec
195	deadreckon run "goal" --sandbox none
196	deadreckon run "goal" --max-spend 5
197	deadreckon run "goal" --max-wall-seconds 1800
198	```
199	
200	`deadreckon run --preview "goal"` prints the provider and model before creating
201	state. `--model` is per-run; `deadreckon config model ...` makes the model
202	default for that provider. For CLI providers, `provider default` means
203	deadreckon delegates model choice to Codex or Claude Code unless you pass
204	`--model`.
205	
206	Spend above `$50` requires confirmation:
207	
208	```bash
209	deadreckon run "large goal" --max-spend 75 --i-know-its-a-lot
210	```
211	
212	## TUI
213	
214	Open the dashboard:
215	
216	```bash
217	deadreckon attach <run-id>
218	```
219	
220	The TUI shows:
221	
222	```text
223	run id, status, phase, goal
224	working directory
225	per-turn timer
226	compact spend/context telemetry
227	wide center-left tool-call/provider activity stream
228	narrow center-right live files being generated
229	bottom supervised process/status panel
230	completed-run Markdown docs view
231	provider activity from live Codex session logs
232	```
233	
234	Keys:
235	
236	```text
237	Ctrl-D   detach without killing the run
238	q        quit
239	Esc      quit
240	Tab      move focus between panels
241	j/k      scroll focused panel
242	PgUp/PgDn scroll focused panel by a page
243	```
244	
245	After a run completes, the TUI footer adds lifecycle actions:
246	
247	```text
248	a        apply a completed worktree run
249	b        abandon/discard a completed worktree run
250	d        toggle formatted RUN-NARRATIVE.md docs in the main panel
251	m        materialize/export a completed copy/fresh artifact
252	e        extend a completed copy/fresh run with a follow-up goal
253	s        show run details
254	```
255	
256	The docs view uses a Markdown parser and ratatui styles for headings, bullets,
257	inline code, fenced code blocks, links, horizontal rules, and task lists. Press
258	`d` again to return to provider activity. Scroll it with the same `j/k`,
259	arrow-key, page-key, and mouse-wheel bindings.
260	
261	The TUI does not start, kill, resume, or undo runs. Use CLI commands for those controls.
262	
263	## Completion Actions
264	
265	Completed `run` and `extend` commands show the same lifecycle actions in the CLI:
266	
267	```text
268	completed action [a apply, b abandon, d docs, s show, q quit]:
269	completed action [m materialize, e extend, d docs, s show, q quit]:
270	```
271	
272	Worktree runs use `a` to squash-apply changes to the current branch or `b` to
273	discard the worktree and temporary branch. Copy/fresh runs use `m` to copy the
274	library artifact into a normal directory, `e` to start a child run from the
275	completed artifact, `d` to read `RUN-NARRATIVE.md`, or `s` to inspect state and lineage. Pass `--no-hints` to
276	`run` or `attach` when scripting.
277	
278	The CLI aliases use friendlier lifecycle names:
279	
280	```bash
281	deadreckon finish latest                            # choose apply or export from run mode
282	deadreckon done latest                              # alias for finish
283	deadreckon export latest --dest ./finished-project   # alias for materialize
284	deadreckon keep latest --autostash --cleanup         # alias for apply
285	deadreckon discard latest                            # alias for abandon
286	deadreckon next                                      # alias for status
287	deadreckon watch latest                              # alias for attach
288	deadreckon stop latest                               # alias for kill
289	deadreckon continue latest                           # alias for resume
290	deadreckon inspect latest                            # alias for show
291	deadreckon docs latest                               # alias for doc
292	deadreckon prune --completed                         # alias for cleanup
293	```
294	
295	`extend` is still available for completed worktree runs from the CLI. It creates
296	a new `dr/...` branch from the parent run's branch, so the follow-up keeps the
297	parent changes without applying them to your checkout first:
298	
299	```bash
300	deadreckon extend <worktree-run-id> "continue with the next change"
301	```
302	
303	## List, Show, Kill, Resume
304	
305	```bash
306	deadreckon list
307	deadreckon list --all
308	deadreckon status
309	deadreckon next
310	deadreckon show <run-id>
311	deadreckon show latest
312	deadreckon inspect latest
313	deadreckon finish latest
314	deadreckon finish latest --dest ./finished-project
315	deadreckon finish latest --autostash --cleanup
316	deadreckon apply <run-id>
317	deadreckon apply <run-id> --autostash
318	deadreckon apply <run-id> --cleanup --no-confirm
319	deadreckon apply <run-id> --strategy merge
320	deadreckon apply <run-id> --strategy cherry-pick --no-confirm
321	deadreckon keep <run-id> --autostash --cleanup
322	deadreckon abandon <run-id>
323	deadreckon discard <run-id>
324	deadreckon abandon <run-id> --keep-branch
325	deadreckon cleanup --completed
326	deadreckon cleanup --stale --force
327	deadreckon cleanup --all --completed --no-confirm
328	deadreckon prune --completed
329	deadreckon kill <run-id>
330	deadreckon stop <run-id>
331	deadreckon kill <run-id> --force
332	deadreckon resume <run-id>
333	deadreckon continue <run-id>
334	deadreckon resume <run-id> --from-turn 2
335	deadreckon resume <run-id> --max-wall-seconds 3600
336	```
337	
338	`finish` is the easiest completion command. For a worktree run it routes to
339	`apply`; for a fresh/copy run it routes to `export`; for an in-place run it
340	prints review, docs, and undo guidance.
341	
342	Re-running `deadreckon apply <run-id>` after the changes are already on the
343	target branch is safe: deadreckon reports `already applied` instead of creating
344	or failing an empty commit. Add `--cleanup` to remove the temporary worktree and
345	branch in that already-applied state.
346	
347	`resume --from-turn N` truncates reconstructed history to turn `N` and continues with turn `N + 1`.
348	
349	## Undo
350	
351	Restore the previous turn snapshot:
352	
353	```bash
354	deadreckon undo --run <run-id>
355	```
356	
357	Restore a specific turn:
358	
359	```bash
360	deadreckon undo --run <run-id> --turn 1
361	```
362	
363	Undo restores the run working directory from `snapshots/turn-<N>/` and records
364	an undo trace. For in-place runs, undo restores the original source path because
365	the agent edited that directory directly.
366	
367	## Acceptance Gates
368	
369	If a run has no custom acceptance spec, `dr-gate` checks that the working directory exists and runs `cargo test` when `Cargo.toml` is present.
370	
371	For custom checks, create:
372	
373	```bash
374	/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/runstate/<scope>/runs/<run-id>/acceptance.yaml
375	```
376	
377	Example:
378	
379	```yaml
380	name: notes check
381	checks:
382	  - kind: file_exists
383	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
384	  - kind: content_match
385	    path: "{working_dir}/notes.md"
386	    pattern: "dead reckoning"
387	  - kind: build_success
388	    cwd: "{working_dir}"
389	```
390	
391	Supported check kinds:
392	
393	```text
394	cargo_test
395	file_exists
396	content_match
397	build_success
398	```
399	
400	The acceptance marker is signed with a run-local nonce. A marker written by the agent is refused.

1	# deadreckon Alpha Design
2	
3	## Product
4	
5	`deadreckon` is a Rust 2024 CLI harness for unattended long-running coding tasks. The default user flow is `deadreckon run <goal>`: create durable run state, select a BYOK provider route, execute turns in a disposable sandbox, write spend/provenance/traces/snapshots after every turn, and make the run attachable, resumable, killable, inspectable, and undoable.
6	
7	The alpha implementation is intentionally local-first. Runtime state defaults to `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/`, and tests or explicit smoke runs can override that with `DEADRECKON_HOME=/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.deadreckon-smoke` so this build process does not write outside the allowed implementation tree.
8	
9	## Reference Patterns
10	
11	- AS-BUILT §3: two-layer split. Rust owns state, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, and gates. Markdown skills under `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/skills/` own agent-facing instructions.
12	- AS-BUILT §4: `state.json` per run, status enum, gap-numbered phase IDs, and `current/<task>.json` run pointers.
13	- AS-BUILT §6: JSON lock records with PID liveness and heartbeat stale reclaim.
14	- AS-BUILT §7-8: atomic promotion/gate markers are written by binary-owned verification, not by model prose.
15	- AS-BUILT §9: per-turn snapshots make bounded rollback possible.
16	- Claude Code mining:
17	  - `/Users/gdc/claude-code-source-code/src/tools/BashTool/bashPermissions.ts` and `shouldUseSandbox.ts` inform command side-effect boundaries and sandbox warning posture.
18	  - `/Users/gdc/claude-code-source-code/src/tools/shared/spawnMultiAgent.ts` informs inherited run context for future sub-agent work; alpha records scope and session lineage but leaves explicit forks to V1.
19	  - `/Users/gdc/claude-code-source-code/src/upstreamproxy/upstreamproxy.ts` informs fail-open provider/proxy setup and child-process environment merging.
20	  - `/Users/gdc/claude-code-source-code/src/ink/renderer.ts` informs ratatui attach rendering: bounded frames, no uncontrolled terminal state.
21	  - `/Users/gdc/claude-code-source-code/docs/prompts/` informs the Markdown skill shape in `skills/default-coding/SKILL.md`.
22	
23	## Workspace
24	
25	Source lives under `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`:
26	
27	- `crates/deadreckon-core`: run paths, phase machine, JSON state, codebase mode records, locks, heartbeats, snapshots, provenance, spend, traces, gates, imports, chains, and run docs primitives.
28	- `crates/deadreckon-runtime`: provider turn loop, sandboxed tool dispatch, cancellation checks, docs polish orchestration, `dr-gate` invocation, and promotion orchestration.
29	- `crates/deadreckon-providers`: BYOK config at `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/config.toml`, provider trait, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible, `cli:claude-code`, `cli:codex`, and explicit `--smoke` scripted adapters, fallback routing, spend estimates.
30	- `crates/deadreckon-sandbox`: `sandbox-exec`, `bwrap`, `docker`, and `none` backends using `tokio::process::Command`; default `auto`.
31	- `crates/deadreckon`: clap parser, command handlers, ratatui attach UI, init/setup, config/settings, run, status/next, list/runs, doc/docs, attach/watch, kill/stop, resume/continue, undo/restore, show/inspect, import, materialize/export, finish/done, apply/keep, abandon/discard, cleanup/prune, extend/follow-up, library/artifacts, chain, and doctor/check.
32	- `skills/default-coding/SKILL.md`: Markdown skill loaded at runtime.
33	- `tests/`: workspace integration tests.
34	
35	## Top-10 Need Mapping
36	
37	1. Live Context & Spend Meter: `spend.jsonl` in `deadreckon-core`, spend summaries in `deadreckon attach`.
38	2. Multi-Agent Worktree Coordination: scope hashing, run pointers, and locks in `deadreckon-core`.
39	3. Infinite Undo For Agent Edits: per-turn `snapshots/turn-<N>/` plus `deadreckon undo`.
40	4. Prompt-To-Code Provenance Audit Trail: `provenance.jsonl` and `deadreckon show`.
41	5. Cross-Tool State Sharing: read-only import from `/Users/gdc/.claude/projects/`, `/Users/gdc/.codex/sessions/`, `/Users/gdc/.cursor/chats/`.
42	6. Agent Observability: `traces.jsonl` with LLM/tool/sandbox events and latencies.
43	7. Disposable Sandboxes: platform-native sandbox backends, Docker opt-in, `none` warning.
44	8. Billing Guardrails: `--max-spend <USD>` pauses runs when durable spend reaches cap.
45	9. Provider Routing / BYOK: adapters, CLI sub-agents, `deadreckon init`, `deadreckon config get/set`, and fallback chain configured from TOML.
46	10. Workspace Inventory & Run Queue: project-scoped `list`, `status`/`next`, `latest` run aliases, `attach`, `kill`, `resume`, `cleanup`, and state scan commands.
47	
48	## Execution Model
49	
50	The primary path is provider-driven: `deadreckon run <goal>` resolves the
51	codebase mode, previews the plan, creates state, and hands execution to
52	`deadreckon-runtime`. The runtime calls `ProviderRouter::complete`, parses model
53	actions, executes tool calls in the configured sandbox, feeds results into
54	history, writes docs, invokes `dr-gate`, and promotes successful runs. It
55	repeats until a provider returns `done`, a spend cap pauses the run, or the run
56	is killed. HTTP providers use user-supplied keys or env vars; CLI providers use
57	local subscription CLIs and run through the deadreckon sandbox wrapper.
58	
59	In a git repo, the default codebase mode is `worktree`: deadreckon creates
60	`~/.deadreckon/worktrees/<scope>-<run-id>` on a `dr/...` branch, runs the agent
61	there, and leaves the user's checkout untouched until `deadreckon apply`. Outside
62	git, interactive users can initialize git, copy the directory, or cancel.
63	Non-interactive users must pass `--fresh`, `--from`, or initialize git first.
64	The former empty working directory path remains available as `--fresh`.
65	
66	For keyless local verification only, `deadreckon run --smoke <goal>` selects the `smoke` provider explicitly. That scripted provider still goes through the same turn loop, sandbox dispatch, snapshots, spend records, traces, provenance, and external `dr-gate` acceptance marker; it is not the default run path.
67	
68	The default skill is Markdown and external to the binary. The binary loads it and records the skill name/path in state; it does not parse or mutate skill internals.
69	
70	## CLI Lifecycle
71	
72	Completed artifacts are promoted into `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/library/<scope>/<run-id>/`.
73	Worktree runs keep their `dr/...` branch available for review and finish with
74	`deadreckon finish <run-id>`, `deadreckon apply <run-id>`, or
75	`deadreckon abandon <run-id>`. `done` aliases `finish`, `keep` aliases `apply`,
76	and `discard` aliases `abandon`. `apply` supports squash, merge, and
77	cherry-pick strategies; `abandon` removes the worktree and, unless
78	`--keep-branch` is used, the temporary branch.
79	
80	Copy and fresh runs use `deadreckon materialize <run-id> --dest <path>` or the
81	`deadreckon export <run-id> --dest <path>` alias to copy the library artifact to
82	a user-owned path. `deadreckon finish <run-id> --dest <path>` routes to the same
83	export behavior for copy/fresh runs. These commands write
84	`.deadreckon/parent.json` and record the reverse `.materialized-to` marker in
85	the library. `deadreckon extend
86	<run-id> "follow-up goal"` preserves the parent's mode semantics: worktree
87	parents create a child `dr/...` branch off the parent branch, copy/fresh parents
88	seed a new working tree from the parent library, and in-place parents refuse with
89	a direct `run --in-place` hint. Extended runs store parent lineage in
90	`working/.deadreckon/parent.json` and start the normal turn loop with reset
91	resource caps.
92	
93	For normal operation, run ids accept unique prefixes and `latest` / `last`
94	resolve to the most recent run in the current project scope. `deadreckon list`
95	defaults to that current scope, `deadreckon list --all` shows global history, and
96	running `deadreckon` without a subcommand is equivalent to `deadreckon status`.
97	`deadreckon cleanup` / `deadreckon prune` remove abandoned, stale, or explicitly
98	selected completed worktree runs while leaving promoted library artifacts in
99	place.
100	
101	Lineage and codebase mode metadata intentionally stay outside `PipelineState`;
102	show/list/hints derive them from marker files and `working/.deadreckon/codebase.json`
103	so the state schema remains stable.
104	
105	Self-documenting run artifacts also live outside `PipelineState`. Each run
106	starts `working/.deadreckon/docs/`, appends deterministic per-turn records, and
107	attempts one `run-narrator` polish pass before promotion unless `--no-docs` is
108	set. Public copies land under `docs/` in the promoted artifact, and `apply`
109	builds its default commit body from the narrative and decisions docs.
110	
111	## Decisions And Conflicts
112	
113	- Runtime writes during verification: the rider prescribes `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/`, while the build instruction forbids edits outside `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/` and `/Users/gdc/stoa/docs/goals/`. The binary defaults to `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/`, but all repository verification uses `DEADRECKON_HOME=/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.deadreckon-smoke`.
114	- Sub-agent forking: the architecture requires the pattern, but the V1 list explicitly moves `deadreckon fork` to V1. Alpha records scope/session lineage and keeps the subprocess skill boundary; explicit multi-agent forks are documented in `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
115	- Sandbox fallback: on macOS `auto` selects `sandbox-exec` if available. If not available, or on Linux without `bwrap`, `doctor` reports the missing binary and `run` falls back to `none` with a warning, matching the rider.
116	- Live Tier C CLI verification: `codex` was run with `exec --ephemeral --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` inside deadreckon's outer `sandbox-exec` wrapper. Run `59c57e4565704135a9982789d0754803` produced `working/notes.md`, `traces.jsonl`, `provenance.jsonl`, snapshots, and a validated `dr-gate` marker without raw API keys.
117	- First-run UX: `deadreckon init` writes `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/config.toml`, `deadreckon config get/set` performs non-interactive edits, `doctor` prints actionable check/fix lines, and `run` enforces the `$50` confirmation guard for scripts.
118	- Codebase modes: the architecture keeps mode metadata in
119	  `working/.deadreckon/codebase.json` rather than extending `PipelineState`.
120	  This preserves existing runstate readers while allowing worktree, copy,
121	  in-place, and fresh flows to evolve independently.
122	- Crate boundary: `deadreckon-core` is adapter-free and owns durable schemas and
123	  primitives. `deadreckon-runtime` owns the dependencies on providers and
124	  sandboxes, so core tests and downstream readers can reason about state without
125	  pulling in HTTP, subprocess, or platform sandbox orchestration.
126

1	# deadreckon Primary Flow Gap Analysis
2	
3	Audit date: 2026-05-11. Scope: `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`.
4	
5	## Primary-Flow Findings
6	
7	| finding | status | evidence |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| Default run was a fixed local script instead of a provider-driven loop. | Resolved. | `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs` calls `ProviderRouter::complete`; Tier B grep confirms no `coding_turn_script`, `hardcoded_smoke`, or `fn smoke_turn` remains under `crates/`. |
10	| Provider router existed but was unused by `run`. | Resolved. | `crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs` builds a router for normal runs, and `run_turn_loop` records `llm.complete` traces per turn. |
11	| No model-to-tool protocol existed. | Resolved. | `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs` accepts JSON `bash`, `write_file`, and `done` actions and feeds tool results into `history.json`. |
12	| CLI sub-agent providers were missing. | Resolved. | `crates/deadreckon-providers/src/cli_claude_code.rs`, `cli_codex.rs`, and `cli_common.rs` implement `cli:claude-code` and `cli:codex`; tests use fake binaries and verify sandbox wrapping. |
13	| `kill` could not interrupt live work. | Resolved for the harness process and sandbox child pids. | `state.json` persists `child_pids`; sandbox/provider pid files live under `child-pids/`; `deadreckon kill` signals both sources and marks status `killed`. |
14	| `resume` did not continue execution. | Resolved. | `deadreckon resume` reloads state/history and re-enters `run_turn_loop`; integration tests verify history survives. |
15	| Anti-self-attestation gate was absent. | Resolved. | `crates/deadreckon/src/bin/dr-gate.rs` writes `proofs/turn-acceptance.json`; core validates `run_id`, producer, and pass status before completion. |
16	| Provenance IDs were not tied to traces. | Resolved. | Tool traces carry `tool_call_id`; provenance records reuse those ids; integration tests assert every provenance id appears in traces. |
17	| Demo cast was hand-authored placeholder output. | Resolved. | `demo.cast` now contains asciicast v2 JSON generated from real release-binary `init/run --provider cli-codex/list/attach/show/undo/kill/resume` output using `DEADRECKON_HOME=/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.deadreckon-smoke`. |
18	| Keyless tests did not prove agentic behavior. | Resolved. | `cargo test --workspace` includes mock OpenAI-compatible provider tests, three-turn integration, kill, resume-history, acceptance-marker, and fake CLI-provider tests. |
19	| Original V0 first-run UX was incomplete. | Resolved. | `deadreckon init`, `deadreckon config get/set`, actionable `doctor`, config-backed spend defaults, high-spend confirmation guards, TUI Ctrl-D detach, and colored spend/context meters are implemented in `crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs` and covered by integration tests. |
20	
21	## Logged Decisions
22	
23	- API keys are not required for Tier A/B verification. The keyless paths are the OpenAI-compatible mock provider in tests and the explicit `--smoke` scripted provider for local release-binary checks.
24	- Tier C was executed with live `cli:codex` using `codex exec --ephemeral` and deadreckon's outer `sandbox-exec` wrapper. The latest successful run id is `f8be423c3cb14a12869206ae25184377`.
25	- `asciinema` is not installed in the current environment. `demo.cast` is therefore generated from captured real command output and kept in asciicast v2 format.
26	- Existing untracked `.cursorindexingignore` is outside the task scope and was not created or modified by deadreckon work.
27	
28	## Alpha Robustness Notes
29	
30	- Cross-process attach cannot consume an in-memory Tokio broadcast from an already running process, so the loop writes every broadcast event to `events.jsonl`; the TUI replays that durable stream at 100 ms cadence.
31	- `doctor` performs exhaustive local checks and actionable provider credential checks. HTTP provider live pings are guarded by `DEADRECKON_DOCTOR_PING=1` to avoid spending user keys during routine local verification.
32

I have what I need. Now I'll evaluate, then write the design doc.

## Evaluation summary

**Command surface** (28 verbs once aliases counted; ~15 unique concepts):
- **Setup**: `init`, `config` (get/set/provider/model), `doctor`
- **Run loop**: `run`, `attach`/watch, `status`/next, `list`/runs, `kill`/stop, `resume`/continue
- **Completed**: `finish`/done, `apply`/keep, `materialize`/export, `extend`/follow-up, `doc`/docs, `library`/artifacts, `show`/inspect
- **Recovery**: `abandon`/discard, `cleanup`/prune, `undo`/restore
- **Other**: `import`, `chain` (serial multi-goal)

**What's strong**
- The killer demo (`--smoke`) works keylessly — instant proof of value.
- `status`/`next` is the perfect one-shot "what now?" verb.
- Aliases are friendly (`finish` beats `apply`+`export` for beginners).
- Worktree-by-default = "your repo is safe" — the headline safety promise.
- README's `Lifecycle:` block in CLI help is excellent.

**What blocks instant value**
1. **Quickstart starts with `cargo build --release`**, not "download this binary." A binary-download user gets stuck on step 1.
2. **20+ verbs surfaced at once** before the user has earned the right to care about most of them. The mental load up-front is "too many tools," not "one new tool."
3. **No "30-second wow"** path — the smoke run is buried as section 6 in README, not section 1.
4. **No habit-loop narrative**. The README is reference-shaped; users don't see themselves kicking off a run at 9am and reviewing at 5pm.
5. **Aliases are advertised next to canonical names** (`finish/done`, `apply/keep`, `kill/stop`…). Pick the friendly one as the default and hide aliases until the user needs them.
6. **The trust contract** (signed gate, provenance) is sold before the user has felt the basic loop — it lands as "feature list" instead of "you'll thank me later."

**The six-command core** a daily user actually types:

```
init     run     next     attach     finish     undo
```

Everything else is recovery, inspection, or power-user. The doc should make this explicit.

Now writing the design doc.

# Getting Started With deadreckon

This is the front door. Read this if you just downloaded the binary and want to feel value in five minutes.

For exhaustive flags and edge cases, see [HOWTO.md](../HOWTO.md). For why the project exists, see the [README](../README.md). This page is the opinionated path from `chmod +x` to "I'm running this every day."

---

## The one-sentence pitch

> deadreckon lets you start a long coding task, walk away, and come back to a reviewable artifact — not a lost terminal.

It wraps the agentic CLI you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Anthropic/OpenAI HTTP) and adds the missing operational layer: isolated workspace, durable state, live attach, spend caps, per-turn undo, and a signed acceptance gate before anything touches your branch.

---

## The 60-second proof (no API key, no config)

You can prove the entire harness works without spending a dollar or wiring up a provider. This is the demo that earns the rest of your attention.

\```bash
deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" --smoke --sandbox none --max-spend 1
deadreckon next
deadreckon doc latest
\```

That sequence runs a deterministic fake provider through the real turn loop. It writes traces, spend, provenance, snapshots, run docs, and a signed acceptance marker — exactly like a real run, just with a scripted "model." If `next` says `completed` and `doc latest` prints a `RUN-NARRATIVE.md`, the binary is healthy.

If anything looks wrong, run `deadreckon doctor` and follow the actionable lines.

---

## The 5-minute first real run

Wire it up to the agentic CLI you already trust, then run a small task on a real project.

### 1. One-time setup

\```bash
deadreckon init           # interactive: pick provider, sandbox, default spend cap
deadreckon doctor         # confirm everything is reachable
\```

The defaults are reasonable: `auto` sandbox, `$10` spend cap, `3600s` wall-clock cap. You can override per run.

If you already have Codex or Claude Code installed and logged in:

\```bash
deadreckon init --provider cli:codex       --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
deadreckon init --provider cli:claude-code --sandbox auto --max-spend 10 --no-confirm
\```

API users:

\```bash
deadreckon init --provider anthropic --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" --no-confirm
deadreckon init --provider openai    --api-key "$OPENAI_API_KEY"    --no-confirm
\```

### 2. Your first real task

`cd` into any git repo, then:

\```bash
deadreckon run "add a CHANGELOG entry for the last 5 commits"
\```

You'll see a preview block (mode, branch, base ref, worktree path), then:

\```
started run a1b2c3d4 (a1b2c3d4...)
attach: deadreckon attach a1b2c3d4
\```

Your checkout is untouched. The agent is working in a separate `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch under `~/.deadreckon/worktrees/`.

### 3. Watch it (optional)

\```bash
deadreckon attach latest
\```

Press `Ctrl-D` to detach without killing it. The run continues even if you close the terminal.

### 4. Finish

When it's done:

\```bash
deadreckon next                              # "completed. try: deadreckon finish latest"
deadreckon doc latest                        # read the narrative
deadreckon finish latest --autostash --cleanup
\```

`finish` does the right thing automatically: for a worktree run it applies the squashed diff to your current branch and removes the temporary worktree.

That's the loop. You now know the product.

---

## The six commands you actually need

Memorize these six. Everything else is recovery, inspection, or power-user surface.

| Verb | When you type it | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `deadreckon init` | Once per machine | Pick provider, sandbox, spend cap |
| `deadreckon run "goal"` | Start of a task | Spawn an isolated agent run |
| `deadreckon next` | Any time | One-line "what's happening, what to do next" |
| `deadreckon attach latest` | When you want to watch | Live TUI; `Ctrl-D` detaches without killing |
| `deadreckon finish latest` | When it's done | Apply (worktree) or export (copy/fresh), with confirmation |
| `deadreckon undo --run latest` | When you regret turn N | Restore the snapshot from before that turn |

Three optional safety verbs for when something feels off:

| Verb | When |
|---|---|
| `deadreckon kill latest` | The run is stuck or burning money |
| `deadreckon resume latest` | A run crashed or you killed it and want to keep going |
| `deadreckon discard latest` | The work was bad; throw it away |

That's it. Nine verbs cover ~95% of real use.

---

## The daily habit loop

deadreckon is built for unattended work, so the right rhythm is "start, walk away, review."

### Morning: kick off the longest thing first

\```bash
deadreckon run "refactor the billing module to use the new Stripe Checkout API"
\```

Print the run id, close the laptop, go to a meeting. The run keeps going whether your terminal is alive or not.

### Mid-day: glance and decide

\```bash
deadreckon next        # "run a1b2c3d4 is running, turn 7, $2.40 spent"
\```

If you want to look closer:

\```bash
deadreckon attach latest   # then Ctrl-D to detach
\```

Kick off a second, smaller run in parallel if you want. deadreckon's scope locks prevent two runs from clobbering the same task.

### End of day: review, apply, or discard

\```bash
deadreckon list                              # what's done?
deadreckon doc latest                        # what did it actually do?
deadreckon finish latest --autostash --cleanup
\```

For runs you don't want:

\```bash
deadreckon discard latest
\```

Weekly:

\```bash
deadreckon cleanup --completed
\```

That's the entire daily loop. Three to five commands a day.

---

## Mental model in one diagram

\```
your repo
  │
  │ deadreckon run "goal"
  ▼
isolated worktree on dr/... branch         ← your checkout is safe
  │
  │ every turn writes: traces, spend,
  │ provenance, snapshot, docs
  ▼
signed acceptance gate                      ← agent can't mark itself done
  │
  ▼
deadreckon finish latest                    ← you decide whether to keep it
  │
  ▼
applied to your branch, with a narrative commit body
\```

The agent owns the coding. deadreckon owns the boundary around the coding.

---

## What's familiar (so you can stop reading)

If you've used these patterns before, deadreckon will feel close to home:

- **`git stash` / `git worktree`** — `run` makes a worktree; `apply` is squash-merge; `discard` is worktree remove.
- **`docker run` then `docker exec`** — `run` then `attach`; `attach` is non-owning, like `docker logs -f`.
- **`make`** — `init` once, then `run`/`finish` is the day-to-day pair.
- **`brew services`** — `list`, `status`, `kill`, `resume` mirror the verbs you already know.
- **A CI build** — every run produces a durable artifact under `~/.deadreckon/library/<scope>/<run-id>/` you can re-inspect later.

---

## When to leave this page

You're ready for the rest of the surface when you've felt one of these:

| You feel… | Read… |
|---|---|
| "I want to chain multiple goals into one supervised job" | [HOWTO.md](../HOWTO.md) → `chain` |
| "I want to extend a completed run with a follow-up" | `deadreckon extend latest "next thing"` ([HOWTO.md](../HOWTO.md)) |
| "I want custom acceptance checks for my project" | [HOWTO.md](../HOWTO.md) → Acceptance Gates |
| "I want to import my old Claude/Codex/Cursor history" | `deadreckon import claude-code` ([HOWTO.md](../HOWTO.md)) |
| "I want to know what's in my run library" | `deadreckon library list` |
| "I want to understand the internals" | [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md), [docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md](AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md) |

---

## The 9-verb cheat sheet

Print this. Tape it next to your keyboard.

\```
SETUP (once)
  deadreckon init                          pick provider, sandbox, spend cap
  deadreckon doctor                        verify everything reachable

DAILY (every day)
  deadreckon run "goal"                    start a run in an isolated worktree
  deadreckon next                          "what's happening, what's next?"
  deadreckon attach latest                 watch live; Ctrl-D detaches
  deadreckon finish latest                 apply (worktree) or export (copy/fresh)

WHEN SOMETHING GOES WRONG
  deadreckon undo --run latest             roll back the last turn
  deadreckon kill latest                   stop a stuck or expensive run
  deadreckon resume latest                 continue an interrupted run
  deadreckon discard latest                throw away a completed run
\```

Nine verbs. One loop. Your repo stays clean.

# Command Surface & Value-Prop Review

Audit date: 2026-05-12. Reviewer: design pass for "downloaded the binary → daily user" conversion.

## TL;DR

deadreckon's product is excellent and its CLI ergonomics are mostly there. The thing blocking instant value is **presentation, not function**. The 30-second proof works (`--smoke`), the daily loop is six commands, the trust contract is real. But the README and `--help` surface them all at the same level of emphasis, so a new user can't tell the core loop apart from recovery, library inspection, history import, or chain orchestration.

The biggest single lift would be to lead every surface (README, `--help`, docs) with the **9-verb core** ([GETTING-STARTED.md](GETTING-STARTED.md) cheat sheet) and demote everything else into a "you'll need this eventually" section.

## What's working

1. **`--smoke` is a gift.** It proves the harness end-to-end without an API key. It should be sentence one of the README, not section six.
2. **`next`/`status` is the perfect single-keystroke verb.** It collapses "what's happening, what should I do" into one line. This is the verb a daily user types most.
3. **Worktree-by-default is the headline safety promise.** "Your checkout is untouched until `finish`" is the sentence that earns trust.
4. **`finish` is the right friendly verb.** Routing worktree → apply and copy/fresh → export removes the mode-distinction tax for beginners.
5. **The `Lifecycle:` blocks inside `--help`** (TOP_LEVEL_HELP, RUN_HELP, etc.) are unusually good. Most CLIs don't teach a flow; deadreckon does.
6. **Aliases match intent.** `keep`/`discard`/`stop`/`continue` read like English. The friendly names should be the canonical names.

## What blocks instant value

### 1. README quickstart starts with `cargo build --release`

Binary-download users aren't building from source. Quickstart should be:

\```bash
deadreckon run "tiny hello rust" --smoke --sandbox none --max-spend 1
\```

…and only mention `cargo build` in a "build from source" appendix.

### 2. Twenty-plus verbs are surfaced at once

The `Command Surface` table in the README and the long alias-pair lists in HOWTO.md ("finish/done", "apply/keep", "kill/stop", "abandon/discard"…) double the apparent complexity. A user counts 28 names and thinks "too much."

**Fix:** lead with the nine-verb core. Move aliases to a single footnote: "every friendly verb has a literal alias; type `--help` to see both."

### 3. No habit-loop narrative

The docs are reference-shaped. A new user can't picture themselves using this at 9am, 1pm, and 5pm. [GETTING-STARTED.md](GETTING-STARTED.md) now fills that gap; consider pulling its "Daily habit loop" section into the README directly.

### 4. The trust contract is sold before the loop is felt

"Signed acceptance gates," "provenance," "self-documenting artifacts" are the long-term reasons to stay. But a brand-new user wants to feel `run → walk away → finish` first. Move the trust section to appear *after* Quickstart, not before.

### 5. Provider setup is shown four ways at once

Init shows `cli:codex`, `cli:claude-code`, `anthropic`, `openai` examples back-to-back. New users freeze. Pick one default per audience (`cli:codex` for subscription users, `anthropic` for API users) and link the rest from a "other providers" line.

### 6. `chain` is a power tool that lives in the main flow

`chain` is impressive but cognitively expensive. Move it to a separate doc (`docs/CHAIN.md`) and keep the main flow about single runs until the user asks for more.

## Concrete README changes (high leverage, low effort)

1. **Replace the Quickstart block** with the `--smoke` line as step 1, then `init` as step 2, then a real `run`.
2. **Add a "Six commands you'll actually type" table** under "Why this exists."
3. **Move the Command Surface listing** to the bottom of the README under "Full surface (you don't need this yet)."
4. **Hide aliases** from the main listing — show `finish` not `finish/done`. Mention the rule once: "every friendly verb has a short alias."
5. **Pin one provider per audience** in the init section; link to HOWTO for the rest.
6. **Link [GETTING-STARTED.md](GETTING-STARTED.md) prominently** above HOWTO.md — it's the right front door once a binary lands.

## The 9-verb core

The verbs a daily user actually types:

\```
SETUP        init, doctor
DAILY        run, next, attach, finish
RECOVERY     undo, kill, resume, discard
\```

Everything else — `show`, `list`, `doc`, `extend`, `materialize`, `apply`, `abandon`, `cleanup`, `library`, `import`, `chain`, `config`, `keep`, `done`, `stop`, `continue`, `inspect`, `discard`, `prune`, `watch`, `restore` — is reachable through `next` hints and `--help` when the user needs it. It should not be on the first page they read.

## The habit-loop summary (one screen)

\```
Morning      deadreckon run "big task"          → walk away
Midday       deadreckon next                    → "still running, $2.40"
             deadreckon attach latest           → glance, Ctrl-D
Evening      deadreckon doc latest              → what did it do?
             deadreckon finish latest           → apply or export
Weekly       deadreckon cleanup --completed     → housekeeping
\```

If this fits on a sticky note, the product becomes a daily habit. If it doesn't, it's a tool you remember to use occasionally. The work above pulls the docs toward the sticky-note version.

Goal met. Two new docs land in the repo:

- **`docs/GETTING-STARTED.md`** — the opinionated front door from binary download to daily habit. Structured as: 1-sentence pitch → 60-second keyless proof (`--smoke`) → 5-minute first real run → 6-command core → daily habit loop (morning/midday/evening) → familiarity bridges (git worktree, docker, brew services) → 9-verb sticky-note cheat sheet.
- **`docs/COMMAND-SURFACE-REVIEW.md`** — the evaluation behind it. What's working (smoke run, `next`, worktree default, `finish`, alias intent, `Lifecycle:` help blocks), six concrete blockers to instant value, and six high-leverage README changes (lead with `--smoke`, demote aliases, hide `chain` from the main flow, pin one provider per audience, link Getting Started above HOWTO).

**Headline finding:** the product is right and the CLI is mostly right — the 9-verb daily loop (`init`, `doctor`, `run`, `next`, `attach`, `finish`, `undo`, `kill`, `resume`, `discard`) is solid. What blocks instant value is presentation: 28 visible verbs at first contact, `cargo build` as quickstart step 1, and the trust contract sold before the loop is felt. The new Getting Started doc fixes the user-facing side; the Review doc gives the team the README-level changes to lift conversion.
